screens.title: Sources and Types of Threat Intelligence
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how organizations gather threat intelligence from both inside and outside their environment, and why mixing sources matters. We begin by defining internal sources such as SIEM, EDR, IDS/IPS, network captures, and human reports that reflect your unique operational context. Then we compare external sources — open, community, and commercial — that expand visibility into global threats and attacker methods. You will see the difference between tactical data like Indicators of Compromise such as IPs and hashes, and more enduring intelligence such as Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures, and complete threat actor profiles. We’ll also cover practical exchange standards like STIX and TAXII and why validation and curation are essential to avoid false positives and alert fatigue. A concrete example you’ll revisit is correlating multiple failed logins in a SIEM, then enriching that signal with external actor information to decide whether to block, investigate, or monitor. By the end you’ll be able to pick the right sources for a scenario, assess their limitations, and outline steps to validate and integrate intelligence into your security operations. How will you combine internal signals and external context to make faster, more accurate decisions?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next screens you'll gain four practical skills. First, you'll identify and differentiate between internal and external intelligence sources so you can select which feeds to trust for a given incident. I'll show how SIEM logs, EDR alerts, NetFlow, and human reports deliver different signals and why internal context matters. Second, you'll evaluate the reliability and relevance of threat intelligence sources. That means learning to spot outdated feeds, incomplete OSINT, and the higher curation levels in commercial services, and deciding when to cross-check. Third, you'll learn the distinction between open-source and commercial intelligence: what OSINT can give you quickly, versus the deeper, validated packages subscription services provide. Finally, you will be introduced to common sharing formats and frameworks such as STIX and TAXII, and why machine-readable exchange enables automated enrichment and faster response. Each objective ties to a competency milestone you can verify by describing value, limitation, and a validation method for a sample source.

screens.title: Internal Sources of Threat Intelligence
screens.narratorSegment: Internal sources are the most context-rich inputs available to a security team. They include SIEM logs that aggregate events, endpoint detection and response alerts that show suspicious process behavior, IDS/IPS signatures and alerts, NetFlow or network traffic captures that reveal unusual connections, authentication servers that record login behavior, and human reports from analysts or help desks. The central benefit is that these sources reflect your actual environment — the systems, user accounts, and configurations you care about — so an indicator here is immediately meaningful. For example, if your SIEM correlates many failed logins from a single external IP across several hosts, then a later successful login from that same IP is a higher-confidence signal of compromise than a single failed attempt alone. A common misconception is to treat internal logs as flawless; in reality, they contain noise, time skew, and missing fields that must be considered during analysis. To use internal data effectively, you need parsing, normalization, and correlation rules, and a process for enrichment with outside context. Key decisions include whether to block traffic immediately, isolate a host, or escalate for investigation. Always ask: does this indicator map to a known user, asset, or business process before taking disruptive action?

keyIdea.title: Context beats raw lists
keyIdea.text: Internal telemetry ties indicators to actual assets and users, making triage and response more accurate and impactful.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.2 › Internal Sources
Internal telemetry stack
SIEM
Aggregates logs and correlates events to reveal patterns across systems.
EDR
Endpoint alerts and process behavior that expose compromise methods.
Network Telemetry
NetFlow and PCAP provide communication context and anomalies.
Human Reports
Analyst observations and help-desk tickets often reveal suspicious emails or behavior.
Explanation & example
  • Internal sources show who and what are affected, enabling targeted response and forensics.
  • Example: a SIEM flags multiple failed logins from one IP, then a successful login — a high-priority lead to investigate for credential compromise.
  • Misconception: treating internal logs as complete; missing telemetry or parsing errors can hide events.
  • Validation step: normalize timestamps, enrich with asset owner, and correlate across EDR and network logs before blocking.
Key Takeaway

Internal intelligence anchors alerts to assets and users, making response more precise.

screens.title: From Internal Signal to Action
screens.narratorSegment: Turning internal signals into effective action requires a repeatable process. Start by detecting a suspicious event: for example, a SIEM rule fires showing multiple failed logins across hosts. Step two is enrichment: gather EDR data for those hosts, check authentication servers for associated accounts, and look at NetFlow captures to see destination IPs. Step three is validation: cross-check whether the external IP appears in known blocklists, whether a credible external feed reports the same actor, and whether the activity matches a known TTP such as credential stuffing. Step four is decision: choose whether to block, isolate, or monitor. A common mistake is immediate blocking based on a single internal indicator without enrichment, which can disrupt legitimate activity. Another error is delaying action because an external feed is not yet confirmed; internal context can justify preliminary containment. To make this reliable, automate enrichment steps where possible and maintain human review for high-impact actions. Practically, a well-tuned process reduces time-to-detection and false positives while preserving business continuity. What small automation could you add to enrich alerts automatically in your environment? From Internal Signal to Action means correlation and enrichment reduce false positives and support measured response decisions.. In practical terms, correlating events, enriching with context, and deciding response. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Enrich before you act
keyIdea.text: Correlation and enrichment reduce false positives and support measured response decisions.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.2 › Signal → Action
4-step response process
  1. Detect: identify suspicious events in SIEM or IDS.
  2. Enrich: pull EDR, NetFlow, and authentication logs for context.
  3. Validate: cross-reference external feeds and known TTPs.
  4. Decide: block, isolate, monitor, or escalate with minimal disruption.
Supporting notes
  • Automate enrichment to add EDR evidence and asset owner before human review.
  • Misconception: immediate blocking is always best — consider business impact first.
  • Use internal context to justify temporary containment when external confirmation is pending.
  • Keep an audit trail of correlation and decisions to refine detection rules later.
Scenario
Multiple failed logins from one IP, then a success. Enrich with EDR and NetFlow to confirm lateral movement before isolating the host.

screens.title: Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT)
screens.narratorSegment: Open-source intelligence refers to information collected from publicly available channels: security blogs, research write-ups, government advisories, social media discussions, public repositories of indicators, and forums. OSINT excels at speed and breadth — many researchers publish early findings about new exploits or active campaigns that give defenders an early warning. For instance, a widely-followed blog post describing a new ransomware variant can prompt rapid patching or policy changes. However, OSINT can also be noisy, contain unverified claims, or include stale indicators. A common pitfall is treating every public IoC as equally reliable; without validation, acting on low-quality OSINT can cause false positives. To protect against this, validate public claims by seeking corroboration from other reputable sources or internal telemetry. Also consider ethical and legal boundaries when monitoring certain forums. OSINT is a powerful tool when used as an early signal and cross-checked before automated blocking. Ask yourself: does this public report include details I can corroborate in my own logs or with a trusted community partner? Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT) means use public reports as early warnings, then corroborate with internal data or trusted feeds before acting.. In practical terms, publicly available sources and their practical uses and limits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.2 › OSINT
What OSINT gives you
  • Early warnings about new vulnerabilities and campaigns.
  • Public IoCs and researcher analysis that can guide immediate checks.
  • Community-driven context that may not yet appear in commercial feeds.
Limitations & precautions
  • Can be noisy, unverified, or stale.
  • May require legal/ethical review for some sources.
  • Always validate before automated blocking to avoid false positives.
Example
A public advisory describes a new exploit being used in the wild. Use it to prioritize patching and then look for confirmatory internal logs or trusted community reports before broad network blocks.

screens.title: Commercial Threat Intelligence Feeds
screens.narratorSegment: Commercial feeds provide curated, contextualized intelligence often produced by vendor analysts and advanced collection methods. These services frequently include validated Indicators of Compromise, actor profiles, and mapped TTPs with higher confidence and timeliness than many open sources. For example, a vendor report may include a validated cluster of IoCs tied to a named actor along with observed techniques and recommended mitigations. The primary trade-off is cost; organizations must assess whether the feed’s depth and accuracy justify the subscription. A typical misconception is that commercial always means flawless — even curated feeds can contain irrelevant or transient indicators. Integration challenges also exist: STIX/TAXII delivery is powerful, but it requires connector work, normalization, and filtering to avoid overwhelming security controls. Use commercial feeds to prioritize strategic and high-confidence response and to enrich internal signals, not as the sole basis for disruptive blocking unless corroborated by internal telemetry. In short, commercial feeds are excellent for strategic and operational context but still require validation and thoughtful integration. Commercial Threat Intelligence Feeds means commercial feeds add context and reliability, but still need integration, filtering, and validation to avoid noise.. In practical terms, what curated, subscription-based intelligence offers compared to osint. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Commercial feeds add context and reliability, but still need integration, filtering, and validation to avoid noise.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.2 › Commercial Feeds
Benefits
  • Analyst-validated indicators and actor context.
  • Detailed TTP descriptions and mitigation guidance.
  • Often delivered in machine-readable formats for automation.
Challenges
  • Subscription cost and integration work.
  • Possible irrelevance to your industry or geography without filtering.
  • Still requires cross-checking with internal evidence to avoid false positives.
Practical tip
Use commercial feeds to enrich high-priority alerts and to inform defensive tuning. Filter for relevance to your assets and geography before automating blocking rules.

screens.title: Indicators of Compromise (IoCs)
screens.narratorSegment: Indicators of Compromise are the tactical, often short-lived data points that security tools use for detection and blocking. Typical IoCs include IP addresses, domain names, file hashes, URLs, and email addresses. They are easy to deploy into automated controls and are valuable for immediate containment. However, IoCs are often ephemeral — adversaries can change infrastructure, rotate domains, or alter files to avoid detection. That means relying on IoCs alone is a fragile strategy. A better approach is to use IoCs for short-term containment while seeking broader context: identify whether the IoC is tied to a larger campaign, whether the behavior matches known TTPs, and whether the indicator appears in trusted feeds or internal telemetry. A common mistake is applying a broad, global blocklist without considering business impact; some IoCs may overlap with shared hosting or third-party services you rely on. The core practice is to automate IoC ingestion but gate high-impact blocking behind enrichment and human review when necessary. Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) means use iocs for quick detection and containment, but enrich and validate to build durable defenses.. In practical terms, tactical, atomic pieces of data used for detection and blocking. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.2 › IoCs
Common IoC types
  • IP addresses (e.g., 192.0.2.1)
  • Domains and URLs
  • File hashes (for example, SHA256 hashes)
  • Email addresses used in phishing campaigns
Operational notes
  • IoCs are ideal for quick signatures and IOC-based blocks.
  • They expire fast; confirm persistence before long-term blocks.
  • Enrich with TTPs and actor context to make decisions more durable.
Example
An IP listed in a public blocklist is a tactical IoC. To elevate it to operational intelligence, seek associated TTPs, actor attribution, or corroborating internal evidence before taking disruptive action.

screens.title: Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs)
screens.narratorSegment: TTPs describe how adversaries operate — the patterns and behaviors they use to achieve objectives — and are more enduring than atomic indicators. Mapping observed activity to a framework such as MITRE ATT&CK helps defenders detect behavior rather than only blocking known IoCs. For example, a detection that focuses on an executable attempting to dump credentials or on lateral movement over administrative channels targets the way attackers act, not the exact file or IP. This behavioral focus reduces the brittleness of defences since techniques persist longer than infrastructure. A frequent misconception is that TTPs are only strategic and not useful for daily operations; in reality, incorporating TTP detection into rules and playbooks materially improves resilience. Use TTPs to design detection logic that looks for suspicious sequences of events, enrich alerts with likely attacker aims, and prioritize mitigations that disrupt the adversary’s methods. When possible, link TTPs to known actor profiles and to IoCs to build a layered, context-rich response. Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) means ttps provide lasting detection value and support defenses that generalize across changing indicators.. In practical terms, behavioral intelligence that outlasts individual indicators. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.2 › TTPs
What TTPs tell you
They describe attacker behavior such as credential theft, lateral movement, or command-and-control techniques. TTPs focus detection on the methods attackers use, not on single-use artifacts.
Operational use
  • Map alerts to known techniques to prioritize response.
  • Design detections for sequences of behaviors rather than isolated artifacts.
  • Enrich TTP findings with IoCs and actor context for decision-making.
Example
Instead of blocking a specific hash, detect the behavior of credential dumping and alert for investigation, which thwarts variants that change their binary but use the same technique.

screens.title: Threat Actor Profiles
screens.narratorSegment: Threat actor profiles aggregate observed behavior, historical campaigns, motivations, and likely targets for specific groups or individuals. These profiles help strategic decisions: what assets are most at risk, what defenses to prioritize, and whether an organization is in scope for particular adversaries. For instance, a profile that documents a group's preference for ransomware with a focus on healthcare targets would raise the priority of backups, network segmentation, and patient-data protections. Profiles often combine TTPs, IoCs, and analysis of motivations and capabilities. A typical misconception is treating actor profiles as definitive; attribution is difficult and sometimes contested. Profiles should be used as guidance to shape risk management and long-term mitigations, not as absolute proof for punitive action. Profiles are valuable when they inform threat models and control design, and when they are updated with fresh intelligence and internal corroboration. Ask: which of our assets would an actor with these capabilities likely target, and what controls would reduce that risk? screens.title: STIX and TAXII: Standards for Sharing
screens.narratorSegment: STIX and TAXII are complementary standards that let systems share structured threat information at scale. STIX is a language for representing threat data — things like indicators, observed behaviors, and actor descriptions — in a structured form. TAXII is the transport mechanism that moves those STIX objects between providers and consumers. Together, they allow a Threat Intelligence Platform or SIEM to automatically pull curated intelligence from a provider and to integrate it into enrichment or detection workflows. The benefit is automated, consistent sharing that reduces manual translation and speeds response. A frequent challenge is integration: receiving systems need parsers, normalization, and filtering to avoid ingesting irrelevant or low-quality data. Another practical risk is automating blocking from unfiltered STIX feeds, which can introduce false positives. To mitigate this, implement validation rules, map STIX objects to local asset inventories, and apply relevance filters by industry, geography, and severity. When done correctly, STIX/TAXII enables faster, more repeatable enrichment and helps teams act on intelligence in minutes rather than hours. screens.title: Validating and Curating Threat Intelligence
screens.narratorSegment: Not all intelligence is suitable for immediate action. Validation and curation are the processes that turn raw data into trustworthy operational intelligence. Start by checking source credibility: is the feed curated by analysts, or is it an unverified community list? Next, corroborate the indicator with internal evidence — can the SIEM or EDR confirm related activity? Then enrich the indicator with context such as asset criticality, affected users, and known TTPs. Apply filters for relevance to your industry and geography, and assign confidence scores that influence automation decisions. A common error is ingesting everything and then suffering alert fatigue; a better pattern is selective ingestion with staged automation: low-confidence indicators create alerts, high-confidence and corroborated indicators can trigger automated containment. Maintain provenance metadata for each indicator so you can audit why a decision was made. Finally, continuously tune these validation rules based on post-incident review and false positive analysis. This curation loop preserves signal quality and ensures your security controls remain effective and trustworthy. screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: First, internal threat intelligence — SIEM, EDR, NetFlow, authentication logs, and analyst reports — provides context you cannot get from external feeds. This context anchors alerts to assets and users and informs safer, more precise responses. Second, external sources come in flavors: OSINT offers rapid public signals, commercial feeds offer curated and validated intelligence often at cost, and ISACs provide sector-specific context. Each has strengths and trade-offs you must weigh for relevance, cost, and timeliness. Third, intelligence types range from tactical IoCs to enduring TTPs and strategic actor profiles. IoCs are useful for immediate detection but are often transient; TTPs and actor profiles support durable defenses and risk management. Together, these concepts form a layered approach: use internal telemetry to validate external intelligence, enrich indicators with TTP and actor context, and apply standards like STIX/TAXII to automate sharing while preserving validation rules.

In this chapter you will learn how organizations gather threat intelligence from both inside and outside their environment, and why mixing sources matters. We begin by defining internal sources such as SIEM, EDR, IDS/IPS, network captures, and human reports that reflect your unique operational context. Then we compare external sources — open, community, and commercial — that expand visibility into global threats and attacker methods. You will see the difference between tactical data like Indicators of Compromise such as IPs and hashes, and more enduring intelligence such as Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures, and complete threat actor profiles. We’ll also cover practical exchange standards like STIX and TAXII and why validation and curation are essential to avoid false positives and alert fatigue. A concrete example you’ll revisit is correlating multiple failed logins in a SIEM, then enriching that signal with external actor information to decide whether to block, investigate, or monitor. By the end you’ll be able to pick the right sources for a scenario, assess their limitations, and outline steps to validate and integrate intelligence into your security operations. How will you combine internal signals and external context to make faster, more accurate decisions?

Over the next screens you'll gain four practical skills. First, you'll identify and differentiate between internal and external intelligence sources so you can select which feeds to trust for a given incident. I'll show how SIEM logs, EDR alerts, NetFlow, and human reports deliver different signals and why internal context matters. Second, you'll evaluate the reliability and relevance of threat intelligence sources. That means learning to spot outdated feeds, incomplete OSINT, and the higher curation levels in commercial services, and deciding when to cross-check. Third, you'll learn the distinction between open-source and commercial intelligence: what OSINT can give you quickly, versus the deeper, validated packages subscription services provide. Finally, you will be introduced to common sharing formats and frameworks such as STIX and TAXII, and why machine-readable exchange enables automated enrichment and faster response. Each objective ties to a competency milestone you can verify by describing value, limitation, and a validation method for a sample source.

This second objectives slide ties each skill to a practical activity. You will practice identifying source value by listing what a SIEM, EDR, NetFlow, and help-desk report reveal about an incident, and you will mark their limitations. You will evaluate an OSINT post and a commercial feed entry, noting timeliness, curation level, and potential for false positives. You will explain when a feed should be cross-checked with internal telemetry before automated blocking. Finally, you will outline steps to receive STIX/TAXII data into a client system and how to validate that data by checking timestamps, actor context, and corroborating indicators. These exercises are designed so you can prove competency by producing a short validation plan for a single suspicious IP, explaining what internal evidence you'd seek and which external sources you would trust. This hands-on orientation helps translate knowledge into operational actions that reduce risk while limiting unnecessary disruption.

Internal sources are the most context-rich inputs available to a security team. They include SIEM logs that aggregate events, endpoint detection and response alerts that show suspicious process behavior, IDS/IPS signatures and alerts, NetFlow or network traffic captures that reveal unusual connections, authentication servers that record login behavior, and human reports from analysts or help desks. The central benefit is that these sources reflect your actual environment — the systems, user accounts, and configurations you care about — so an indicator here is immediately meaningful. For example, if your SIEM correlates many failed logins from a single external IP across several hosts, then a later successful login from that same IP is a higher-confidence signal of compromise than a single failed attempt alone. A common misconception is to treat internal logs as flawless; in reality, they contain noise, time skew, and missing fields that must be considered during analysis. To use internal data effectively, you need parsing, normalization, and correlation rules, and a process for enrichment with outside context. Key decisions include whether to block traffic immediately, isolate a host, or escalate for investigation. Always ask: does this indicator map to a known user, asset, or business process before taking disruptive action?

Turning internal signals into effective action requires a repeatable process. Start by detecting a suspicious event: for example, a SIEM rule fires showing multiple failed logins across hosts. Step two is enrichment: gather EDR data for those hosts, check authentication servers for associated accounts, and look at NetFlow captures to see destination IPs. Step three is validation: cross-check whether the external IP appears in known blocklists, whether a credible external feed reports the same actor, and whether the activity matches a known TTP such as credential stuffing. Step four is decision: choose whether to block, isolate, or monitor. A common mistake is immediate blocking based on a single internal indicator without enrichment, which can disrupt legitimate activity. Another error is delaying action because an external feed is not yet confirmed; internal context can justify preliminary containment. To make this reliable, automate enrichment steps where possible and maintain human review for high-impact actions. Practically, a well-tuned process reduces time-to-detection and false positives while preserving business continuity.
